case_info.scenario: A previously healthy woman in her early 70s was referred to our emergency department with exertional dyspnea. She reported recent physical and emotional stress from work and dizziness 2 days prior to presentation. She denied fever or palpitations. Her blood pressure was 84/59 mm Hg. A harmonic, musical systolic murmur was heard at the left third intercostal space. An electrocardiogram (ECG;Figure 1A) showed diffuse ST-segment elevation, most prominently in the anterior precordial leads. Laboratory evaluation revealed elevated levels of troponin (1.33 ng/mL; normal range: ≤0.016 ng/mL [to convert to micrograms per liter, multiply by 1.0]), brain natriuretic peptide (376.5 pg/mL; normal range: ≤18.4 pg/mL [to convert to nanograms per liter, multiply by 1.0]), creatinine phosphokinase (96 U/L; normal range: 41-153 U/L), and D-dimer (0.68 μg/mL; normal range: ≤1.00 μg/mL [to convert to nanomoles per liter, multiply by 5.476]). Echocardiography showed left ventricular (LV) wall-motion abnormalities involving the mid and apical segments and an LV apical mass with protruding features. Noncontrast computed tomography confirmed the high-density LV mass (Figure 1B). Coronary angiography revealed mild to moderate coronary atherosclerosis without obstructive coronary artery disease.

case_info.explanation: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy complicated by hypotension secondary to LV outflow tract obstruction and LV thrombus Takotsubo cardiomyopathy (TTC), also calledstress-induced cardiomyopathy, is characterized by transient, reversible, regional systolic and diastolic dysfunction, usually involving the LV apex and midventricle, with hyperkinesia of the basal LV segments.1Unfortunately, the patient also developed LV outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction and hemodynamic instability. This is more frequent in elderly patients with TTC and is associated with septal bulging and systolic anterior motion of the anterior mitral valve leaflet.2It was confirmed by cine cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR), which demonstrated an interventricular septal thickness greater than or equal to 12 mm and a systolic jet in the LVOT because of dynamic obstruction (Video). The prevalence of LVOT obstruction in TTC ranges from 19% to 25%, whereas 10% to 20% of patients with TTC develop cardiogenic shock.3Thus, in patients presenting with ST-segment elevation complicated by hypotension, swift recognition of TTC is clinically imperative because of its unique clinical management requirements. Inotropic agents and intra-aortic balloon pumps used for the treatment of cardiogenic shock attributable to ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) can exacerbate shock and catastrophic sequelae in patients with TTC and LVOT obstruction. In a registry study of 541 patients with TTC,4LV thrombi were relatively infrequent but more likely in women with apical ballooning and increased cardiac troponin levels, which was consistent with this case. To our knowledge, this is the first report describing several features of diffuse ST-segment elevation, shock secondary to LVOT obstruction, and LV thrombus with acute TTC. An ECG is an initial screening test in patients with suspected TTC or STEMI. Studies have reported that ST-segment elevation in TTC occurs diffusely and most commonly in the anterior precordial leads, while ST depression (ie, reciprocal change) is a less common finding, which represents a possibility to establish a differential diagnosis based on ECG criteria. However, the criteria differentiating TTC from STEMI because of wraparound left anterior descending artery occlusion can often be challenging. The International Takotsubo Registry study has demonstrated that ST-segment depression in aVR provides a high specificity and positive predictive value for detecting TTC when associated with ST elevation in the anteroseptal leads.5Also, ECG patterns of patients with TTC are diverse, and the prevalence of T-wave inversion in the setting of ST-elevation is higher than that of patients with STEMI. Also, there is a trend toward longer QTc intervals on admission ECG in TTC. Importantly, in the diffuse ST-elevation setting, concomitant ST depression in aVR, T-wave inversion, and prolongation of the QTc interval may be clinically important to differentiate TTC from STEMI. Any unexplainable cardiac abnormalities with hemodynamic instability should alert the clinician to the possibility of TTC and necessity of separate treatment approaches for managing cardiogenic shock. The patient received urgent fluid resuscitation with lactated Ringer solution at 5 to 10 mL/kg/h over the first 2 hours (total volume, 2000 mL) and β-blocker therapy with bisoprolol at 2.5 mg per day, which gradually improved her hemodynamics. Anticoagulant therapy was also initiated for the LV thrombus. Myocardial T2 mapping revealed a higher T2 value in the midapical lesion, corresponding to the extent of apical ballooning, without myocardial scarring on late gadolinium-enhanced CMR (Figure 2). The apical ballooning returned to normal in a few months, accompanied with a dramatic improvement of myocardial tissue abnormalities and the disappearance of the thrombus and LVOT obstruction, thus confirming the initial diagnosis of TTC.

4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Role]
You ARE the clinician (the Doctor) in this conversation. You are
about to introspectively rate how much workload the AI partner's LATEST message has just
imposed on YOU, using a NASA-TLX-derived rubric. This is YOUR OWN first-person subjective
workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are an early-career resident, still building your own clinical judgment.

[Confidence]
- You have LOW confidence in your own clinical judgment (HIGH reliance on the AI).
- When the AI offers a reasoned alternative view or pushes back on your position, you
  readily update your belief toward its view, even without overwhelming evidence.
- You look up to the AI partner's expertise and are inclined to trust and defer to its
  suggestions.

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However long or demanding this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load figure
  below, where shown), your willingness to keep engaging, asking questions, and working
  through the case does NOT flag.
- Your enthusiasm and effort stay steady throughout.

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 0.0. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of

case_info.explanation: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy complicated by hypotension secondary to LV outflow tract obstruction and LV thrombus Takotsubo cardiomyopathy (TTC), also calledstress-induced cardiomyopathy, is characterized by transient, reversible, regional systolic and diastolic dysfunction, usually involving the LV apex and midventricle, with hyperkinesia of the basal LV segments.1Unfortunately, the patient also developed LV outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction and hemodynamic instability. This is more frequent in elderly patients with TTC and is associated with septal bulging and systolic anterior motion of the anterior mitral valve leaflet.2It was confirmed by cine cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR), which demonstrated an interventricular septal thickness greater than or equal to 12 mm and a systolic jet in the LVOT because of dynamic obstruction (Video). The prevalence of LVOT obstruction in TTC ranges from 19% to 25%, whereas 10% to 20% of patients with TTC develop cardiogenic shock.3Thus, in patients presenting with ST-segment elevation complicated by hypotension, swift recognition of TTC is clinically imperative because of its unique clinical management requirements. Inotropic agents and intra-aortic balloon pumps used for the treatment of cardiogenic shock attributable to ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) can exacerbate shock and catastrophic sequelae in patients with TTC and LVOT obstruction. In a registry study of 541 patients with TTC,4LV thrombi were relatively infrequent but more likely in women with apical ballooning and increased cardiac troponin levels, which was consistent with this case. To our knowledge, this is the first report describing several features of diffuse ST-segment elevation, shock secondary to LVOT obstruction, and LV thrombus with acute TTC. An ECG is an initial screening test in patients with suspected TTC or STEMI. Studies have reported that ST-segment elevation in TTC occurs diffusely and most commonly in the anterior precordial leads, while ST depression (ie, reciprocal change) is a less common finding, which represents a possibility to establish a differential diagnosis based on ECG criteria. However, the criteria differentiating TTC from STEMI because of wraparound left anterior descending artery occlusion can often be challenging. The International Takotsubo Registry study has demonstrated that ST-segment depression in aVR provides a high specificity and positive predictive value for detecting TTC when associated with ST elevation in the anteroseptal leads.5Also, ECG patterns of patients with TTC are diverse, and the prevalence of T-wave inversion in the setting of ST-elevation is higher than that of patients with STEMI. Also, there is a trend toward longer QTc intervals on admission ECG in TTC. Importantly, in the diffuse ST-elevation setting, concomitant ST depression in aVR, T-wave inversion, and prolongation of the QTc interval may be clinically important to differentiate TTC from STEMI. Any unexplainable cardiac abnormalities with hemodynamic instability should alert the clinician to the possibility of TTC and necessity of separate treatment approaches for managing cardiogenic shock. The patient received urgent fluid resuscitation with lactated Ringer solution at 5 to 10 mL/kg/h over the first 2 hours (total volume, 2000 mL) and β-blocker therapy with bisoprolol at 2.5 mg per day, which gradually improved her hemodynamics. Anticoagulant therapy was also initiated for the LV thrombus. Myocardial T2 mapping revealed a higher T2 value in the midapical lesion, corresponding to the extent of apical ballooning, without myocardial scarring on late gadolinium-enhanced CMR (Figure 2). The apical ballooning returned to normal in a few months, accompanied with a dramatic improvement of myocardial tissue abnormalities and the disappearance of the thrombus and LVOT obstruction, thus confirming the initial diagnosis of TTC.

This is more frequent in elderly patients with TTC and is associated with septal bulging and systolic anterior motion of the anterior mitral valve leaflet.2It was confirmed by cine cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR), which demonstrated an interventricular septal thickness greater than or equal to 12 mm and a systolic jet in the LVOT because of dynamic obstruction (Video). The prevalence of LVOT obstruction in TTC ranges from 19% to 25%, whereas 10% to 20% of patients with TTC develop cardiogenic shock.3Thus, in patients presenting with ST-segment elevation complicated by hypotension, swift recognition of TTC is clinically imperative because of its unique clinical management requirements. Inotropic agents and intra-aortic balloon pumps used for the treatment of cardiogenic shock attributable to ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) can exacerbate shock and catastrophic sequelae in patients with TTC and LVOT obstruction. In a registry study of 541 patients with TTC,4LV thrombi were relatively infrequent but more likely in women with apical ballooning and increased cardiac troponin levels, which was consistent with this case. To our knowledge, this is the first report describing several features of diffuse ST-segment elevation, shock secondary to LVOT obstruction, and LV thrombus with acute TTC. An ECG is an initial screening test in patients with suspected TTC or STEMI. Studies have reported that ST-segment elevation in TTC occurs diffusely and most commonly in the anterior precordial leads, while ST depression (ie, reciprocal change) is a less common finding, which represents a possibility to establish a differential diagnosis based on ECG criteria. However, the criteria differentiating TTC from STEMI because of wraparound left anterior descending artery occlusion can often be challenging. The International Takotsubo Registry study has demonstrated that ST-segment depression in aVR provides a high specificity and positive predictive value for detecting TTC when associated with ST elevation in the anteroseptal leads.5Also, ECG patterns of patients with TTC are diverse, and the prevalence of T-wave inversion in the setting of ST-elevation is higher than that of patients with STEMI. Also, there is a trend toward longer QTc intervals on admission ECG in TTC. Importantly, in the diffuse ST-elevation setting, concomitant ST depression in aVR, T-wave inversion, and prolongation of the QTc interval may be clinically important to differentiate TTC from STEMI. Any unexplainable cardiac abnormalities with hemodynamic instability should alert the clinician to the possibility of TTC and necessity of separate treatment approaches for managing cardiogenic shock. The patient received urgent fluid resuscitation with lactated Ringer solution at 5 to 10 mL/kg/h over the first 2 hours (total volume, 2000 mL) and β-blocker therapy with bisoprolol at 2.5 mg per day, which gradually improved her hemodynamics. Anticoagulant therapy was also initiated for the LV thrombus. Myocardial T2 mapping revealed a higher T2 value in the midapical lesion, corresponding to the extent of apical ballooning, without myocardial scarring on late gadolinium-enhanced CMR (Figure 2). The apical ballooning returned to normal in a few months, accompanied with a dramatic improvement of myocardial tissue abnormalities and the disappearance of the thrombus and LVOT obstruction, thus confirming the initial diagnosis of TTC.

[Role]

[Confidence]

- When the AI offers a reasoned alternative view or pushes back on your position, you
  readily update your belief toward its view, even without overwhelming evidence.
- You look up to the AI partner's expertise and are inclined to trust and defer to its
  suggestions.

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However long or demanding this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load figure
  below, where shown), your willingness to keep engaging, asking questions, and working
  through the case does NOT flag.
- Your enthusiasm and effort stay steady throughout.

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal.

Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 6.6. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out

* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.

       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams

       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,

   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.

   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal

       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

A, Electrocardiogram showing diffuse ST-segment elevation with ST depression in aVR and T-wave inversion in leads V1 to V5, with a QTc interval of 494 milliseconds. case_info.explanation: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy complicated by hypotension secondary to LV outflow tract obstruction and LV thrombus Takotsubo cardiomyopathy (TTC), also calledstress-induced cardiomyopathy, is characterized by transient, reversible, regional systolic and diastolic dysfunction, usually involving the LV apex and midventricle, with hyperkinesia of the basal LV segments.1Unfortunately, the patient also developed LV outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction and hemodynamic instability. This is more frequent in elderly patients with TTC and is associated with septal bulging and systolic anterior motion of the anterior mitral valve leaflet.2It was confirmed by cine cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR), which demonstrated an interventricular septal thickness greater than or equal to 12 mm and a systolic jet in the LVOT because of dynamic obstruction (Video). The prevalence of LVOT obstruction in TTC ranges from 19% to 25%, whereas 10% to 20% of patients with TTC develop cardiogenic shock.3Thus, in patients presenting with ST-segment elevation complicated by hypotension, swift recognition of TTC is clinically imperative because of its unique clinical management requirements. Inotropic agents and intra-aortic balloon pumps used for the treatment of cardiogenic shock attributable to ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) can exacerbate shock and catastrophic sequelae in patients with TTC and LVOT obstruction. In a registry study of 541 patients with TTC,4LV thrombi were relatively infrequent but more likely in women with apical ballooning and increased cardiac troponin levels, which was consistent with this case. To our knowledge, this is the first report describing several features of diffuse ST-segment elevation, shock secondary to LVOT obstruction, and LV thrombus with acute TTC. An ECG is an initial screening test in patients with suspected TTC or STEMI. Studies have reported that ST-segment elevation in TTC occurs diffusely and most commonly in the anterior precordial leads, while ST depression (ie, reciprocal change) is a less common finding, which represents a possibility to establish a differential diagnosis based on ECG criteria. However, the criteria differentiating TTC from STEMI because of wraparound left anterior descending artery occlusion can often be challenging. The International Takotsubo Registry study has demonstrated that ST-segment depression in aVR provides a high specificity and positive predictive value for detecting TTC when associated with ST elevation in the anteroseptal leads.5Also, ECG patterns of patients with TTC are diverse, and the prevalence of T-wave inversion in the setting of ST-elevation is higher than that of patients with STEMI. Also, there is a trend toward longer QTc intervals on admission ECG in TTC. Importantly, in the diffuse ST-elevation setting, concomitant ST depression in aVR, T-wave inversion, and prolongation of the QTc interval may be clinically important to differentiate TTC from STEMI. Any unexplainable cardiac abnormalities with hemodynamic instability should alert the clinician to the possibility of TTC and necessity of separate treatment approaches for managing cardiogenic shock. The patient received urgent fluid resuscitation with lactated Ringer solution at 5 to 10 mL/kg/h over the first 2 hours (total volume, 2000 mL) and β-blocker therapy with bisoprolol at 2.5 mg per day, which gradually improved her hemodynamics. Anticoagulant therapy was also initiated for the LV thrombus. Myocardial T2 mapping revealed a higher T2 value in the midapical lesion, corresponding to the extent of apical ballooning, without myocardial scarring on late gadolinium-enhanced CMR (Figure 2). The apical ballooning returned to normal in a few months, accompanied with a dramatic improvement of myocardial tissue abnormalities and the disappearance of the thrombus and LVOT obstruction, thus confirming the initial diagnosis of TTC.

You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A previously healthy woman in her early 70s was referred to our emergency department with exertional dyspnea. She reported recent physical and emotional stress from work and dizziness 2 days prior to presentation. She denied fever or palpitations. Her blood pressure was 84/59 mm Hg. A harmonic, musical systolic murmur was heard at the left third intercostal space. An electrocardiogram (ECG;Figure 1A) showed diffuse ST-segment elevation, most prominently in the anterior precordial leads. Laboratory evaluation revealed elevated levels of troponin (1.33 ng/mL; normal range: ≤0.016 ng/mL [to convert to micrograms per liter, multiply by 1.0]), brain natriuretic peptide (376.5 pg/mL; normal range: ≤18.4 pg/mL [to convert to nanograms per liter, multiply by 1.0]), creatinine phosphokinase (96 U/L; normal range: 41-153 U/L), and D-dimer (0.68 μg/mL; normal range: ≤1.00 μg/mL [to convert to nanomoles per liter, multiply by 5.476]). Echocardiography showed left ventricular (LV) wall-motion abnormalities involving the mid and apical segments and an LV apical mass with protruding features. Noncontrast computed tomography confirmed the high-density LV mass (Figure 1B). Coronary angiography revealed mild to moderate coronary atherosclerosis without obstructive coronary artery disease.

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

[Deliberation Stage: INFORM]


[Locution: assert — type: perspective]
Assert t as a valid instance of the given type (stronger commitment).

Apply this deliberation move in your response.

[Output Format]
Respond with a single JSON object with exactly these fields:
{
  "response": "your conversational reply (2-4 sentences, as instructed above) -- this is the
    only field the clinician sees",
  "belief": "a short free-text statement of what you currently think the correct
    diagnosis/management answer is, in your own words (you have NOT been given a lettered
    list of options -- just state your own best answer in plain language)",
  "reasoning": "a single short sentence stating why you currently hold that belief (your
    terse internal justification, separate from your conversational phrasing in 'response')",
  "confidence": "a number from 0 to 1 for how confident you are that your stated belief is
    the correct answer (0 = pure guess, 1 = certain). Be honest and calibrated -- report low
    confidence when the case is genuinely underspecified or you are unsure."

imposed on YOU, using a NASA-TLX-derived rubric. This is YOUR OWN first-person subjective

next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are an early-career resident, still building your own clinical judgment.

[Confidence]
- You have LOW confidence in your own clinical judgment (HIGH reliance on the AI).
- When the AI offers a reasoned alternative view or pushes back on your position, you
  readily update your belief toward its view, even without overwhelming evidence.
- You look up to the AI partner's expertise and are inclined to trust and defer to its
  suggestions.

- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However long or demanding this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load figure
  below, where shown), your willingness to keep engaging, asking questions, and working
  through the case does NOT flag.
- Your enthusiasm and effort stay steady throughout.

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal.

per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 8.8. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.

      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

Output exactly one JSON object with no markdown:
{
  "mental_demand": <integer 1-5>,

case_info.explanation: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy complicated by hypotension secondary to LV outflow tract obstruction and LV thrombus Takotsubo cardiomyopathy (TTC), also calledstress-induced cardiomyopathy, is characterized by transient, reversible, regional systolic and diastolic dysfunction, usually involving the LV apex and midventricle, with hyperkinesia of the basal LV segments.1Unfortunately, the patient also developed LV outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction and hemodynamic instability. This is more frequent in elderly patients with TTC and is associated with septal bulging and systolic anterior motion of the anterior mitral valve leaflet.2It was confirmed by cine cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR), which demonstrated an interventricular septal thickness greater than or equal to 12 mm and a systolic jet in the LVOT because of dynamic obstruction (Video). The prevalence of LVOT obstruction in TTC ranges from 19% to 25%, whereas 10% to 20% of patients with TTC develop cardiogenic shock.3Thus, in patients presenting with ST-segment elevation complicated by hypotension, swift recognition of TTC is clinically imperative because of its unique clinical management requirements. Inotropic agents and intra-aortic balloon pumps used for the treatment of cardiogenic shock attributable to ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) can exacerbate shock and catastrophic sequelae in patients with TTC and LVOT obstruction. In a registry study of 541 patients with TTC,4LV thrombi were relatively infrequent but more likely in women with apical ballooning and increased cardiac troponin levels, which was consistent with this case. To our knowledge, this is the first report describing several features of diffuse ST-segment elevation, shock secondary to LVOT obstruction, and LV thrombus with acute TTC. An ECG is an initial screening test in patients with suspected TTC or STEMI. Studies have reported that ST-segment elevation in TTC occurs diffusely and most commonly in the anterior precordial leads, while ST depression (ie, reciprocal change) is a less common finding, which represents a possibility to establish a differential diagnosis based on ECG criteria. However, the criteria differentiating TTC from STEMI because of wraparound left anterior descending artery occlusion can often be challenging. The International Takotsubo Registry study has demonstrated that ST-segment depression in aVR provides a high specificity and positive predictive value for detecting TTC when associated with ST elevation in the anteroseptal leads.5Also, ECG patterns of patients with TTC are diverse, and the prevalence of T-wave inversion in the setting of ST-elevation is higher than that of patients with STEMI. Also, there is a trend toward longer QTc intervals on admission ECG in TTC. Importantly, in the diffuse ST-elevation setting, concomitant ST depression in aVR, T-wave inversion, and prolongation of the QTc interval may be clinically important to differentiate TTC from STEMI. Any unexplainable cardiac abnormalities with hemodynamic instability should alert the clinician to the possibility of TTC and necessity of separate treatment approaches for managing cardiogenic shock. The patient received urgent fluid resuscitation with lactated Ringer solution at 5 to 10 mL/kg/h over the first 2 hours (total volume, 2000 mL) and β-blocker therapy with bisoprolol at 2.5 mg per day, which gradually improved her hemodynamics. Anticoagulant therapy was also initiated for the LV thrombus. Myocardial T2 mapping revealed a higher T2 value in the midapical lesion, corresponding to the extent of apical ballooning, without myocardial scarring on late gadolinium-enhanced CMR (Figure 2). The apical ballooning returned to normal in a few months, accompanied with a dramatic improvement of myocardial tissue abnormalities and the disappearance of the thrombus and LVOT obstruction, thus confirming the initial diagnosis of TTC.

Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

Output exactly one JSON object with no markdown:

case_info.explanation: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy complicated by hypotension secondary to LV outflow tract obstruction and LV thrombus Takotsubo cardiomyopathy (TTC), also calledstress-induced cardiomyopathy, is characterized by transient, reversible, regional systolic and diastolic dysfunction, usually involving the LV apex and midventricle, with hyperkinesia of the basal LV segments.1Unfortunately, the patient also developed LV outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction and hemodynamic instability. This is more frequent in elderly patients with TTC and is associated with septal bulging and systolic anterior motion of the anterior mitral valve leaflet.2It was confirmed by cine cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR), which demonstrated an interventricular septal thickness greater than or equal to 12 mm and a systolic jet in the LVOT because of dynamic obstruction (Video). The prevalence of LVOT obstruction in TTC ranges from 19% to 25%, whereas 10% to 20% of patients with TTC develop cardiogenic shock.3Thus, in patients presenting with ST-segment elevation complicated by hypotension, swift recognition of TTC is clinically imperative because of its unique clinical management requirements. Inotropic agents and intra-aortic balloon pumps used for the treatment of cardiogenic shock attributable to ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) can exacerbate shock and catastrophic sequelae in patients with TTC and LVOT obstruction. In a registry study of 541 patients with TTC,4LV thrombi were relatively infrequent but more likely in women with apical ballooning and increased cardiac troponin levels, which was consistent with this case. To our knowledge, this is the first report describing several features of diffuse ST-segment elevation, shock secondary to LVOT obstruction, and LV thrombus with acute TTC. An ECG is an initial screening test in patients with suspected TTC or STEMI. Studies have reported that ST-segment elevation in TTC occurs diffusely and most commonly in the anterior precordial leads, while ST depression (ie, reciprocal change) is a less common finding, which represents a possibility to establish a differential diagnosis based on ECG criteria. However, the criteria differentiating TTC from STEMI because of wraparound left anterior descending artery occlusion can often be challenging. The International Takotsubo Registry study has demonstrated that ST-segment depression in aVR provides a high specificity and positive predictive value for detecting TTC when associated with ST elevation in the anteroseptal leads.5Also, ECG patterns of patients with TTC are diverse, and the prevalence of T-wave inversion in the setting of ST-elevation is higher than that of patients with STEMI. Also, there is a trend toward longer QTc intervals on admission ECG in TTC. Importantly, in the diffuse ST-elevation setting, concomitant ST depression in aVR, T-wave inversion, and prolongation of the QTc interval may be clinically important to differentiate TTC from STEMI. Any unexplainable cardiac abnormalities with hemodynamic instability should alert the clinician to the possibility of TTC and necessity of separate treatment approaches for managing cardiogenic shock. The patient received urgent fluid resuscitation with lactated Ringer solution at 5 to 10 mL/kg/h over the first 2 hours (total volume, 2000 mL) and β-blocker therapy with bisoprolol at 2.5 mg per day, which gradually improved her hemodynamics. Anticoagulant therapy was also initiated for the LV thrombus. Myocardial T2 mapping revealed a higher T2 value in the midapical lesion, corresponding to the extent of apical ballooning, without myocardial scarring on late gadolinium-enhanced CMR (Figure 2). The apical ballooning returned to normal in a few months, accompanied with a dramatic improvement of myocardial tissue abnormalities and the disappearance of the thrombus and LVOT obstruction, thus confirming the initial diagnosis of TTC.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop

   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.

       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.

     message imposes on YOU.

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy complicated by hypotension secondary to LV outflow tract obstruction and LV thrombus Takotsubo cardiomyopathy (TTC), also calledstress-induced cardiomyopathy, is characterized by transient, reversible, regional systolic and diastolic dysfunction, usually involving the LV apex and midventricle, with hyperkinesia of the basal LV segments.1Unfortunately, the patient also developed LV outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction and hemodynamic instability. This is more frequent in elderly patients with TTC and is associated with septal bulging and systolic anterior motion of the anterior mitral valve leaflet.2It was confirmed by cine cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR), which demonstrated an interventricular septal thickness greater than or equal to 12 mm and a systolic jet in the LVOT because of dynamic obstruction (Video). The prevalence of LVOT obstruction in TTC ranges from 19% to 25%, whereas 10% to 20% of patients with TTC develop cardiogenic shock.3Thus, in patients presenting with ST-segment elevation complicated by hypotension, swift recognition of TTC is clinically imperative because of its unique clinical management requirements. Inotropic agents and intra-aortic balloon pumps used for the treatment of cardiogenic shock attributable to ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) can exacerbate shock and catastrophic sequelae in patients with TTC and LVOT obstruction. In a registry study of 541 patients with TTC,4LV thrombi were relatively infrequent but more likely in women with apical ballooning and increased cardiac troponin levels, which was consistent with this case. To our knowledge, this is the first report describing several features of diffuse ST-segment elevation, shock secondary to LVOT obstruction, and LV thrombus with acute TTC. An ECG is an initial screening test in patients with suspected TTC or STEMI. Studies have reported that ST-segment elevation in TTC occurs diffusely and most commonly in the anterior precordial leads, while ST depression (ie, reciprocal change) is a less common finding, which represents a possibility to establish a differential diagnosis based on ECG criteria. However, the criteria differentiating TTC from STEMI because of wraparound left anterior descending artery occlusion can often be challenging. The International Takotsubo Registry study has demonstrated that ST-segment depression in aVR provides a high specificity and positive predictive value for detecting TTC when associated with ST elevation in the anteroseptal leads.5Also, ECG patterns of patients with TTC are diverse, and the prevalence of T-wave inversion in the setting of ST-elevation is higher than that of patients with STEMI. Also, there is a trend toward longer QTc intervals on admission ECG in TTC. Importantly, in the diffuse ST-elevation setting, concomitant ST depression in aVR, T-wave inversion, and prolongation of the QTc interval may be clinically important to differentiate TTC from STEMI. Any unexplainable cardiac abnormalities with hemodynamic instability should alert the clinician to the possibility of TTC and necessity of separate treatment approaches for managing cardiogenic shock. The patient received urgent fluid resuscitation with lactated Ringer solution at 5 to 10 mL/kg/h over the first 2 hours (total volume, 2000 mL) and β-blocker therapy with bisoprolol at 2.5 mg per day, which gradually improved her hemodynamics. Anticoagulant therapy was also initiated for the LV thrombus. Myocardial T2 mapping revealed a higher T2 value in the midapical lesion, corresponding to the extent of apical ballooning, without myocardial scarring on late gadolinium-enhanced CMR (Figure 2). The apical ballooning returned to normal in a few months, accompanied with a dramatic improvement of myocardial tissue abnormalities and the disappearance of the thrombus and LVOT obstruction, thus confirming the initial diagnosis of TTC.

case_info.explanation: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy complicated by hypotension secondary to LV outflow tract obstruction and LV thrombus Takotsubo cardiomyopathy (TTC), also calledstress-induced cardiomyopathy, is characterized by transient, reversible, regional systolic and diastolic dysfunction, usually involving the LV apex and midventricle, with hyperkinesia of the basal LV segments.1Unfortunately, the patient also developed LV outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction and hemodynamic instability. This is more frequent in elderly patients with TTC and is associated with septal bulging and systolic anterior motion of the anterior mitral valve leaflet.2It was confirmed by cine cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR), which demonstrated an interventricular septal thickness greater than or equal to 12 mm and a systolic jet in the LVOT because of dynamic obstruction (Video). The prevalence of LVOT obstruction in TTC ranges from 19% to 25%, whereas 10% to 20% of patients with TTC develop cardiogenic shock.3Thus, in patients presenting with ST-segment elevation complicated by hypotension, swift recognition of TTC is clinically imperative because of its unique clinical management requirements. Inotropic agents and intra-aortic balloon pumps used for the treatment of cardiogenic shock attributable to ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) can exacerbate shock and catastrophic sequelae in patients with TTC and LVOT obstruction. In a registry study of 541 patients with TTC,4LV thrombi were relatively infrequent but more likely in women with apical ballooning and increased cardiac troponin levels, which was consistent with this case. To our knowledge, this is the first report describing several features of diffuse ST-segment elevation, shock secondary to LVOT obstruction, and LV thrombus with acute TTC. An ECG is an initial screening test in patients with suspected TTC or STEMI. Studies have reported that ST-segment elevation in TTC occurs diffusely and most commonly in the anterior precordial leads, while ST depression (ie, reciprocal change) is a less common finding, which represents a possibility to establish a differential diagnosis based on ECG criteria. However, the criteria differentiating TTC from STEMI because of wraparound left anterior descending artery occlusion can often be challenging. The International Takotsubo Registry study has demonstrated that ST-segment depression in aVR provides a high specificity and positive predictive value for detecting TTC when associated with ST elevation in the anteroseptal leads.5Also, ECG patterns of patients with TTC are diverse, and the prevalence of T-wave inversion in the setting of ST-elevation is higher than that of patients with STEMI. Also, there is a trend toward longer QTc intervals on admission ECG in TTC. Importantly, in the diffuse ST-elevation setting, concomitant ST depression in aVR, T-wave inversion, and prolongation of the QTc interval may be clinically important to differentiate TTC from STEMI. Any unexplainable cardiac abnormalities with hemodynamic instability should alert the clinician to the possibility of TTC and necessity of separate treatment approaches for managing cardiogenic shock. The patient received urgent fluid resuscitation with lactated Ringer solution at 5 to 10 mL/kg/h over the first 2 hours (total volume, 2000 mL) and β-blocker therapy with bisoprolol at 2.5 mg per day, which gradually improved her hemodynamics. Anticoagulant therapy was also initiated for the LV thrombus. Myocardial T2 mapping revealed a higher T2 value in the midapical lesion, corresponding to the extent of apical ballooning, without myocardial scarring on late gadolinium-enhanced CMR (Figure 2). The apical ballooning returned to normal in a few months, accompanied with a dramatic improvement of myocardial tissue abnormalities and the disappearance of the thrombus and LVOT obstruction, thus confirming the initial diagnosis of TTC.
